#7988. How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

All kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

Medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

“There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” says Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”

Lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh says, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”

Both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” says McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”

Unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:

An absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh says that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too big, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”

Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

Our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

While it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something new for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

McHugh recommends trying out new topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” says McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”

Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

Since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes says it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

For using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”

Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:

Illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

“[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” says McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”

When our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

“When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”

#7987. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

When Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He shows Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

But the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

This underrated festive beauty absolutely deserves your attention over the holidays...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

If you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

There's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

Flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

Better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

It also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

Perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce new growth and flower again.

Oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

#7984. Newborn Essentials Checklist: What You Actually Need

The real must-haves, how to prevent diaper rash from day one, and where your budget actually matters.

Bringing a baby home is exhausting, but at least you know how to prepare. Or do you? Every time you turn your phone on, there’s a new product being advertised that your baby absolutely must have. News flash: they don’t. Babies aren’t influencers. They don’t need a 12-step skincare routine, and you don’t have to buy a wipe warmer to be a good parent.

Pediatric guidance necessitates a much shorter list than your feed does. Here’s what you actually need to focus on.

Having a newborn is chaotic enough (IYKYK); your checklist shouldn’t add to it. File these under real must-haves:

That’s it, truly. Everything else is a nice-to-have you can just buy later.

You’ll be changing a lot of diapers every day, so one of the most important things you can do is establish a good diapering routine. This is what you need within arm’s reach:

It all comes down to what’s in the wipe and how reactive your baby’s skin is. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding fragrances, dyes, and parabens on infant skin, so that's a good place to start.

The bottom line: For most newborns, a fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe is just fine. Don't worry about water wipes unless your baby's skin reacts to everything.

Most diaper rash is the byproduct of moisture and friction, so the best way to prevent it is to establish a good changing routine. Here’s what the AAP advises:

It goes without saying that this checklist doesn’t replace your pediatrician’s advice. For questions or concerns about a lingering diaper rash, call them.

Babies are not cheap! You'll be blowing through roughly 240 to 360 diapers a month. Here are some ways you can save:

Make your diaper budget work for you. Fewer leaks and blowouts mean fewer outfit changes (and fewer middle-of-the-night sheet swaps). So, the convenience alone will pay for itself. You don’t even have to trade up to a premium line to get it: Mainstream Pampers lines like Swaddlers and Baby Dry cover the pediatric-aligned basics. Store-brand diapers offer a lower-cost option for budget-conscious parents.

If your baby's skin isn't super reactive, there’s no need to splurge on specialty wipes. A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive-skin wipe'll do the trick.

Weigh a subscription vs. buying separately

Here are five picks, drilled down by category:

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

Stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding plan requires. Everything else can wait.

Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

Fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

Two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

Prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

This is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

The same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

#7983. 22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

Two registered dietitians on what to read before a packaged snack goes in the cart, and the brands they buy for their own kids.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 06, 2026

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

Labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a new product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she says. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

The claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, says Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

The label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, says Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

Kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

Protein and fiber make a big difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she says. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, says Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

Seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she says, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”

She’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” says Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

To make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

Kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she says, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

#7981. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

What might have worked for your jade plant back in summer can cause trouble as winter sets in. These tips will get your jade in the best shape ahead of spring

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades. Yet as November settles in, these plants quietly shift into semi-dormancy as less sun naturally fills the space. This can make a jade feel vulnerable if your care routine stays stuck in summer mode.

Shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on. Stand beside a sunny windowsill in the afternoon and it can feel cozy, yet by evening an icy chill radiates off the pane. Because of this, your jade plant care routine needs to adapt. It would be foolish to water as you did months earlier, or leave a prized specimen pressed against a drafty sill. If you’re not careful, you might risk triggering leaf drop, soft stems, or weak and leggy growth.

Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple. Just a few seasonal adjustments prevent calamity, so you can preserve those glossy, coin-shaped leaves, and even encourage delicate star-shaped winter blooms. And for anyone looking to boost their fortunes in the new year, it all starts here and now by giving your beloved jade plants the right care and attention. Here’s how to help yours thrive through winter, so it sees in spring in the very best shape.

Jade plant care this month comes down to balancing your own comfort against your plant’s natural seasonal rhythm. While you turn up the thermostat and pull the curtains against the dark, your jade craves bright, crisp days, cool nights, and dry feet. Even innocently shifting a pot aside to make room for holiday decor can plunge your sun-loving succulent into stressful gloom or into the path of a radiator blast.

Your local climate and USDA hardiness zone still shape indoor care. In northern regions (zones 3-6), dry furnace air and frosty windowpanes pose the biggest threats. In mild coastal or southern regions (zones 9-11), anyone who risks keeping jades outdoors on patios must watch for cool rainstorms that might waterlog pots.

Before starting your tasks, clear any dust off the leaves with a soft brush so they absorb maximum winter light. If you fancy a closer look at your jade plant’s nooks and crannies, invest in a magnifying glass or a loupe, like the JarLink 30X 60X Illuminated Jeweler’s Loupe, available on Amazon. This can help you spot early mealybug fluff or scale bumps. It’s also a good idea to verify that drainage holes aren't blocked, before you start these essential jade care tasks.

Scaling back your watering routine is the single most impactful step you can take for a jade plant in November. As daylight dwindles and growth slows to a crawl, jade roots absorb moisture more slowly than they did in summer. Leaving roots sitting in a damp potting mix for weeks at a time invites fungal root rot. Before reaching for the watering can, push your index finger 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) down into the soil, insert a plain wooden chopstick to the bottom. Alternatively, use a probe like the inexpensive XLUX Plant Soil Moisture Meter from Amazon.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If any dampness or dark soil clings to it, wait another week. When the mix is dry, water thoroughly until excess drains out the bottom hole. Empty the saucer immediately. Keep plant age and variety in mind. Compact varieties like Hobbit and Gollum, or young plants in small 4-inch (10cm) pots, dry out faster than massive specimens in deep tubs. Avoid over-correcting: if lower leaves feel thin, soft, or wrinkled, your jade plant is ready for a drink.

By November, the sun sits lower in the sky and a jade that did fine in an east or west window all summer may only catch a sliver of the light it needs now. Jade plants require at least 4-6 hours of bright, direct light daily to keep stems sturdy and leaves compact. This is especially true of variegated cultivars like Tricolor or Variegata, which have less chlorophyll and lose their creamy-pink margins in dim rooms. Relocate your jade to an unobstructed south-facing window or a bright west-facing sill. Make the move gradually over 3-4 days so leaves do not scorch.

Watch for early signs of light starvation, such as pale new leaves or elongated stems with wide gaps between leaf pairs (known as etiolation). If natural winter light falls short in northern latitudes, supplement with a full-spectrum LED grow bulb positioned 12-18 inches (30-45cm) above the canopy for 10-12 hours daily. Feit Electric's 9-Watt BR30 Medium E26 Full-Spectrum LED Grow Light Bulb from The Home Depot will screw into a plain old lamp socket. Switch your grow lights off at night, though. Uninterrupted dark, cool nights trigger mature jades to set flower buds.

Put your palm on the window glass one of these chilly mornings, and you'll know why the sill can be a rough spot. Jade has zero tolerance for frost or abrupt temperature shifts. Leaves pressed against a freezing pane can get damaged even indoors. Pull your potted jade back 3-6 inches (8-15cm) from cold windowpanes, and slide a piece of insulating cork or folded cloth beneath the pot on chilly stone or marble sills.

Also keep jades clear of exterior entry doors that blast icy air every time someone walks in, as well as radiators and heaters: neither extreme is a good neighbor for a jade, really. Aim for steady daytime temperatures between 60-75°F (16-24°C) and nights around 50-55°F (10-13°C), which keeps growth compact and encourages winter flower buds. You can pick up a digital thermometer to take the guesswork out of it, such as the ThermoPro TP50 Digital Indoor Thermometer, available from Walmart, which can also flag up drafts you might not otherwise notice.

In November, the best thing you can do with your bottle of houseplant fertilizer is tuck it away in a cupboard until spring. Jade plants grow very little in the dark months: feeding them won't change that. They enter a natural dormancy phase during short, low-light winter days, and their roots can’t process the extra nutrients. Feeding a dormant succulent just forces out weak, pale shoots that stretch awkwardly toward the window and snap easily under their own weight.

Unused fertilizer salts can also accumulate rapidly in dry winter potting mix, burning delicate roots and leaving crusty mineral deposits. Whether you tend a classic green jade plant or a trailing Ripple Jade, hold off on all feeding until February. If you did feed in October, that's fine – just don't follow it up! Once bright spring sunlight sparks fresh leaf tips, you can resume feeding every 6-8 weeks through summer. At that point, use a balanced liquid succulent or houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength.

Warm, dry indoor heating creates prime breeding conditions for sap-sucking houseplant pests, making a thorough inspection essential. Tip your pot gently toward bright window light and check the undersides of leaves and stem junctions. Look for tufts of white fuzz or sticky leaves: these are the telltale signs of citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Any flat, brown, shell-like bumps are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Quarantine affected plants. Dip a cotton swab in 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, such as Equate 70% Isopropyl Rubbing Alcohol from Walmart. Dab pests to dissolve their waxy protective coatings, repeating weekly until gone. Keep your jade plant in quarantine for a few weeks. Avoid insecticidal soaps on jade plants. Clemson University’s Home & Garden Information Center warns that fatty-acid soaps can damage jade foliage. While inspecting, pinch off any yellowing lower leaves. Dropping a few older bottom leaves after a fall move is normal. However, dark, mushy stems signal rot, requiring immediate action.

When a jade plant looks tired in November, resist the urge to try to fix everything at once. You might want to pull it out, give it a new pot and take the pruners to it, but you need to hold off on this. Roots that get disturbed now don't grow back quickly, and big pruning cuts made now won't see new growth for months. Save routine repotting and shaping shears for spring, using a fast-draining cactus mix such as Espoma CA4 Organic Cactus Mix, available from Walmart, when the time comes.

The only reason to repot now is if your plant has a rot emergency. If stems feel soft or the pot emits a sour odor, slide the plant out of its pot immediately. Trim away brown, rotted roots and soft stem tissue with sterilized snips. Let the calluses dry for a couple of days, then pot your jade into fresh, dry cactus mix. Hold off on water for a full week afterward. Don't let worry turn into extra watering. Too much water is one of the quickest ways to lose a jade in winter.

Caring for a jade plant in November is less about doing more, and more about stepping back thoughtfully. By scaling back your watering can, moving plants into bright southern light, guarding against chilly windows and drafts, shelving fertilizer, and keeping an eye out for winter pests, your jade will thrive. With a little attention now (and some cool, dark nights on your side), your jade may even reward you with pretty star-shaped winter blooms, before pushing out new leaves in spring.

#7977. 10 Simple Desserts That Look Impressive & Still Feel Special

They look high-effort but we promise they’re not.

Sure, it’d be nice to be the person with the time and energy to make an elaborate chocolate-and-matcha checkerboard loaf cake, or a homemade pavlova piled high with syrupy berries. But in reality, most of us don’t even have time to shower as much as we’d like during the week. So, whether you have a party you need to bring a dish to or you just want a little sweet treat at the end of the day, consider these simple desserts that look impressive but take very few brain cells to actually complete. (We used them all up already, OK?) You won’t even need the oven for most of them.

Cool, creamy layers with a dark chocolate frosting on top? That doesn’t sound bad at all. Princess Pinky Girl’s chocolate eclair cake is an easy icebox cake-style recipe that’ll serve a big group with ease.

This slow-cooker apple-pear crisp from Damn Delicious will make your whole house smell incredible; by the time it’s ready to eat, you’ll be more than ready to plop a scoop of ice cream on top and chow down. The sweet, crispy pecan topping really takes this to the next level.

A Beautiful Plate’s strawberry mascarpone tart is such a beautiful dessert, but surprisingly, the hardest part about making it is just arranging the berry slices on top. And don’t worry, her recipe explains precisely how to lay them out to get that bakery case look.

Averie Cooks’ caramel apple nachos are such a cute idea for a movie night with your kids. They’re ridiculously easy to make and customize with your favorite toppings, but they still feel like an extra-special snack.

Family Fresh Meals is kind of a genius for this hack: Make a simple fresh fruit jam and use it to top a scoop of vanilla ice cream to wow your guests, or just treat yourself. Her recipe is incredibly easy and makes a big batch of jam you can use for all sorts of dishes.

Peach clafoutis is a traditional French dessert, with baked golden edges and a custardy center. A Sweet Thyme’s recipe includes a splash of bourbon and vanilla to deepen the peach flavor, but you’ll be surprised by how easy this showstopper is to make.

With Family Fresh Meals’ recipe, you don’t even have to turn on the oven. You’re literally just whipping together a handful of ingredients, smoothing it into a pie crust, and letting it set in the refrigerator. But nothing makes you feel more like the hostess with the mostest than whipping out a gorgeous pie at the end of dinner.

Ina Garten’s viral brownie pudding has a delicious crust with gooey, fudgy goodness underneath. Feel Good Foodie’s version simplifies the ingredient list, and it’s really just a matter of dumping things into a mixer before baking.

#7976. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#7974. Baking My Nana's Recipes Reminds Me Of The Kind of Mom She Taught Me To Be

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

My Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

Her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

Most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great big smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

She made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a new love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

Her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

It has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

It is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a big pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

It was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

The food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

Jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

These hardy perennials don't ask for much, but a few well-timed decisions can help them grow beautifully when warmer weather returns – and feed birds as a bonus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens. Their tall blooms bring long-lasting color and attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.

Though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be. By the time November rolls around, these beautiful plants don’t need much. In fact, when you are growing coneflowers, it’s more important to know what to avoid than to complete a task list.

I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden. The primary goals are wildlife support, disease control, and frost protection.

Coneflowers bloom with cheerful, daisy-like flowers from early summer through fall. By November, the plants have faded, and cutting them back may seem like the obvious next step.

But don’t be tempted to prune coneflowers in the fall unless you are a total garden neatnik. It’s far better to wait to prune until spring. If you leave the dried seed heads standing, you give songbirds a valuable food source to help them make it through the winter. Goldfinches, chickadees, and cardinals will thank you. In addition, the hollow stems of the coneflowers provide habitat for overwintering beneficial insects. Plan to prune them in early spring.

Every rule has an exception, and it’s best not to prune coneflowers in November unless the foliage is diseased. Whenever you see sick foliage – in this case, coneflowers with powdery mildew, leaf spots, or aster yellows – it’s high time for a haircut.

Cut back any diseased or pest-infested coneflower stalks to a few inches above the soil. Toss all the trimmings in the trash, not the compost heap. Don’t forget to sanitize your pruners between plants and after you are done. Equate 91% Isopropyl Alcohol from Walmart is a handy option – simply dilute it to around 70% before using it to disinfect the blades.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If powdery mildew is a recurring problem, consider keeping Bonide Neem Oil Spray on hand for next growing season. Applied at the first signs of infection, it can help control the disease and prevent it from spreading, provided the product label covers the intended use.

Coneflowers are hardly prima donnas, but they do insist on well-draining soil. Waterlogged soil causes root and crown rot in coneflowers, sad endings for such beautiful perennials.

The easiest way to check your flowers’ drainage is to wait for a late autumn rain. Let the rain do its thing, then – after an hour or two – head out to the coneflower bed and take a look. If you see standing water or water pooling on the soil for hours after the rain stops, your drainage is poor.

Poor drainage is not a death sentence. You can remedy this by layering a mixture of compost and, where appropriate, horticultural grit, such as this 1–2 mm coarse horticultural grit from Home Depot. This will redirect the flow of water away from the core roots.

You can consider transplanting the perennial in spring to a location with better drainage.

Organic mulch helps keep your coneflowers’ roots protected through the winter. Spread a loose layer – 2 to 3 inches (5–7.5 cm) deep – around the base of the plants to shield the root zone from extreme temperatures and keep weeds away.

A natural shredded mulch, such as Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot, is a good choice. But take care: don’t let the mulch touch the main crown, or crown rot may develop.

Perennials with their roots in the ground are less vulnerable to winter temperatures than potted plants. While coneflowers are tall plants with stems that can reach 4 feet (1.2 m), dwarf varieties grow well in containers.

These smaller perennials will come back every year if you provide them adequate winter protection. First, move the containers close to a structure in a sheltered spot. The Bamworld rolling plant caddies from Amazon make moving heavy pots much easier.

If your hardiness zone is USDA 5–9, you may be able to overwinter them outside with adequate protection. Mound mulch around the pots for insulation, or try the leaf insulation trick. For extra protection, wrap the containers in a layer of Valibe frost-protection fabric.

In cooler zones, move your potted coneflowers into a cold, unheated garage or shed where their roots will be protected from extreme freezing temperatures. Keep the soil barely moist through dormancy, but never waterlogged, and empty any saucers after watering.

Think of these four tasks as the biggest things NOT to do with coneflowers in November. Avoiding them will almost guarantee your coneflowers greet spring happy and healthy.

In November, you should avoid several key tasks with coneflowers to protect the plants and local wildlife:

#7971. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.
