Potted citrus can't usually stay outside once the cold sets in, but the trip inside is hard on them too. A few quick checks can keep leaves on and bugs out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun. Then the cold arrives. Citrus can't take a hard freeze, so in colder climates, potted trees have to come inside for winter.

The move itself is a shock, though. Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after. Indoor light is weaker, the air is drier, and pests that rode in on the branches can spread to nearby houseplants.

That goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike. Six checks before the tree comes through the door can head off much of that.

Most citrus can be damaged below 32°F (0°C), and a potted tree is more exposed than one in the ground. Lemons and limes are usually the most tender, while kumquats, satsumas, and calamondins can handle a little more chill. Aim to have the tree inside before nights start dipping into the 40s (4–9°C). Wait for the first freeze warning, and you'll be dragging a heavy pot from full sun straight indoors. Give it a week or two in a shady spot near the house first instead – it adjusts to lower light that way.

Flip the leaves over and look along the midvein. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) shows up there as small, flat, tan bumps. Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) leave pale speckles and, eventually, fine webbing where the leaf meets the stem, and white, cottony clumps in the leaf joints usually mean citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri).

If you find anything, spray the tree outdoors with an insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil labeled for citrus, such as Monterey horticultural oil concentrate. Plan on more than one round. Once inside, keep it away from other houseplants for three or four weeks.

Bugs don't only ride in on the leaves. Tip the pot on its side, look in the drainage holes, and lift the saucer. Slugs, sowbugs, and earwigs all like that damp spot underneath, and ants sometimes leave small piles of potting mix they've hauled out. A slow soak with the hose drives many of them out.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Check any roots poking through the holes, too. Firm, light-colored roots are a good sign, but dark, mushy ones and a sour smell point to waterlogged soil. Unless the roots are in real trouble, wait to repot citrus trees until spring.

Citrus needs far more light than a pothos or snake plant. Indoors, aim for at least six hours of bright light a day. A south- or southwest-facing window is usually the best spot, with the tree close to the glass but not touching it. Up north, short winter days often fall short – that's when a grow light helps. Glowrium sells a dual-head LED grow light on Amazon that's just under 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, with heads that bend toward the canopy. Trees moved from full sun to a dim corner overnight often shed a good share of their leaves.

Hold a hand over a heating vent or radiator when the heat kicks on. That hot, dry air blows straight across the leaves of a nearby tree, and a cold, drafty window or door is no better. Sudden swings like those commonly trigger leaf drop. Somewhere around 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night, about 55–65°F (13–18°C), works well.

Humidity near 50% helps in a heated house. The Pure Enrichment MistAire humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours on a tank, and the ThermoPro digital hygrometer can sit by the pot to track both.

On a hot patio, potted citrus can need water every day or two. Indoors, with cooler rooms and less light, it uses much less, and the summer routine can drown the roots. Push a finger about 2 inches (5 cm) into the mix, and water only when it feels dry at that depth. Deep pots are harder to judge, which is where a moisture meter, like the Xlux Long Probe Plant Soil Moisture Meter, is invaluable.

Water until some drains out, then empty the saucer. Set the pot on a few terra-cotta Pot Toes to keep the drainage holes clear. Don't overcorrect, though – a tree left bone dry for long stretches drops flowers and can lose leaves.

Some leaf drop in the first few weeks is common. Less light, drier air, and new temperatures all hit at once, and a few leaves on the floor are just part of it, mostly.

Look closer if leaves keep falling after the first month or whole branches go bare. A wet, sour-smelling mix points to overwatering, while a mix that's dry all the way down means it went too long between drinks. Check how close the tree sits to a vent or cold door, and whether that window is as bright in December as it seemed in October. Sticky spots, webbing, or cottony clumps under the leaves mean pests got past the quarantine.

Get through those six checks, and your tree has an easier winter ahead. Come spring, once nights stay above 50°F (10°C), it can head back out to the patio a little at a time.

His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7932. AJ McLean Is The Better Man

AJ McLean, the singer, songwriter, and most tattooed member of The Backstreet Boys just moved his family to New York City. “All three of the ladies in my life love New York,” he says — and he’s all about it. “Celebrating Christmas in New York this year is going to be fantastic.”

But before he can take the family to the Rockettes, McLean has an album to launch (Sex, Love, and Music, out Nov. 27) and a solo tour to rock (The Better Man Tour). He is also busy as the spokesman for Delsym 12-Hour Cough Relief, which he says saved a performance during The Backstreet Boys residency at The Sphere last year. McLean took a break from his tour to take Fatherly’s Cool Dad questionnaire — and talk about staying healthy, sober, and putting family first.

I think I am a cool dad. I think I'm a cool dad because I really kind of let my kids form their own opinions and have a voice, and we work as a team. I want my girls to always have a voice. That's super important to me. Sometimes, they have too much of a voice, but it's OK. That's when dad has to step in and reel it back a little bit. I want my girls to just always look up to their dad, and I try to set the best example that I can.

AJ McLean on his solo “The Better Man” Tour

So I'm an ’80s kid and I am so happy that I turned my girls onto Labyrinth, which they absolutely love; The Goonies, which they absolutely love; and Gremlins. They are obsessed, especially with Labyrinth. When I mentioned it to them, they were a little hesitant, and then once we watched it, I went back to work and caught wind from the wife that they've watched it repeatedly days after, and I'm like, "Yes, I did it."

What's one thing you wish your kids had today that you had growing up, especially as a kid from the ’80s?

I wish they had cassette tape players. I did get a cassette tape player gift box from my boys over at Aerosmith, and it came with a cassette tape of their new album — it was a promotional thing. And I showed it to my daughters, and they did not know what they were looking at. They put it in backwards. I'm like, "No, no, no, no, no, no." And then they were like, "What is the red button?" I said, "No, that's for recording." And they were astounded when I pressed play and this little speaker was playing and I'm like, "When your dad was growing up, that was it. That's all we had. There was no Bose surround sound, there was none of that."

And then my youngest — last year as a birthday present from one of her friends — got a Discman. And she of course put the CD in upside down, I had to show her the right way. That was painful. But she really loves her freaking Discman. She loves it. And I love that they're starting to come back where you actually have to buy the CD. I keep telling my girls, "There's pictures in there; there's thank yous; there's a whole thing. It's not just listening to the music; it's a whole package deal, where you don't get that if you're listening to iTunes. You see one picture and listen to the music, that's it. Albums were a thing." So I'm starting to get them into that now, which I really love.

What's music have you successfully introduced your kids to?

My oldest daughter's first album was The Beatles’ White Album. She learned every word between the ages of 2 and 3. And she was a sponge. My wife is the biggest Beatles fan out of anyone I've ever met in my life. She is diehard. So that was her first album. She's like, "This is what my kids are listening to, Beatles." I'm like, "OK."

AJ McLean and his family, pictured here in 2022, recently moved to New York City.

And what music have your kids introduced you to?

Recently, I took the family to the premiere of Michael, and my daughters knew who Michael Jackson was, but after the film, the obsession was over the top. They know songs I've never heard, deep cuts. People forget about Michael's Jackson’s Xscape album and they're saying, "Dad, play such and such a song." And I'm like, "That's not a song." They're like, "Yes, it is." They know more music, I think, now than I've ever known in my entire life. We have a very musical family, very musical family.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

Fatherhood, to me, means protection. It means compassion, understanding. It means listening with my ears and not my mouth, and being nonjudgmental, which I'm a very nonjudgmental person anyways, but just by nature, that's how I was raised. And trying to really broaden my daughters’ spectrum of the world, and to love everyone, and to accept everyone, and to be colorblind, to be genderblind, to be just very open and loving. And they are. They are two of the coolest kids I think any father could ever ask for. They are super smart. They are loving kids. They are people, people like me.

They're not shy by any means. They will talk to everybody and talk their ear off, and I have no idea where they get that from. But yeah, I try to just really set an example, especially as a father and as a man, I want my daughters to look at me and then be able to say when the time comes that they want to date boys, this is what a boy should be. This is what a man should be, like, respectful. And I grew up single-parent household, so I grew up to very much so respect women to the utmost, and put them up on a pedestal, which it's kind of a give and take, but to really know that none of us would be here without a woman, let's just say that.

What piece of clothing or gear are you really passionate about right now? What do you can't get enough of?

I mean, I'm a sneakerhead. I have a problem. And I've gotten my girls into it now, which my wife is so thrilled about.

Well, it's easier for me because I'm done. My foot's where it's at, it ain't going up, it ain't going down, but my daughters are still growing. So when I go get a pair of Jordans that are like $200 and then my kids want to match daddy's shoes, it's a little like they're going to be in them for six months and then they're going to be out of them. But then we donate them anyway, so we're not just throwing them out; we're donating them.

What are you wearing right now then? What's on your feet?

Right now, I've got my travel shoes, which are my Adidas Ultraboost, but my everyday shoes are [Jordan] 1s or 3s. That is my go-to. My collection has gotten pretty large. And my daughters now, they're nowhere near as many as me, but they're starting to catch up.

I think she loves my heart, my generosity, my kindness, my ability to be very comforting and loving. I'm a very affectionate person. I try to be a very loyal person. I try to be a very honest person. I have my faults; nobody's perfect. I tell people I'm perfectly imperfect. And I think she just loves me for me. I think even more so now, being sober for over five years and living my true authentic self, our relationship now I think is the best it's ever been, being in each other's lives for 15 years.

We went through some tough stuff. We separated, we were living separately, and we both now can look back and reflect on what needed to happen. There are no mistakes. Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

Our house cats retain this same physiology and lack of interest in hunting down fresh water. The problem? They arenât typically chowing down on juicy rodents a dozen times a day. Which means they often donât get the moisture they need to keep those specialized kidneys healthy.

This is why 40% of cats over 10 years old and 80% of cats over 15 years old develop chronic kidney disease. After a lifetime of chronic dehydration, their kidneys simply canât keep up.

One solution is to increase the amount of water cats consume through their food by offering wet food or adding water to their dry food. This is doable if you are home during meal times every day. But if you work long hours, have a million other things to juggle, or occasionally (or often) travel, feeding moist meals consistently becomes more of a challenge.

While these work in the short term, they hold only a limited amount of food (generally between three and six meals) and require a lot of cleanup and constant restocking.

For those who travel or already struggle to get everything done in a day, this is far from being a convenient or effective solution.

The Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder combines the health benefits of a wet-food diet with the convenience and high-capacity of a dry-food automatic feeder.

Unlike traditional automatic wet food feeders that can only store a handful of meals, the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder can hold weeks of food at a time and dispense meals up to every hour, keeping kitties with even the most specialized dietary needs happy and hydrated throughout the day.

Rather than canned or wet packaged food, the Riko works with freeze-dried cat food. This shelf-stable food is ground up into portions, mixed with water, and allowed to rehydrate before serving.

No refrigeration or constant refilling needed. Just fill the hopper with a bag of freeze-dried food of your choice, add filtered water to the reservoir, set the amounts and feeding schedule on the app, and take a well-deserved break from fretting over your catâs meals and hydration status.

#7929. This ‘unhinged’ advice for toddler moms is actually pretty genius

We've all earned our stripes, and sometimes there's nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 13, 2026

Toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in. Some came from toddler room teachers, longtime nannies and even doctors. Most came from moms who’ve logged countless hours negotiating with toddlers and consulting their pediatricians. We’ve all earned our stripes, and sometimes there’s nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

Many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged. And certainly no one’s judging.

Anyone who has turned around in a parking lot to find an empty space where a small person used to be knows this particular brand of panic. The thread’s most-liked reply, with nearly 18,000 hearts, went straight at the escape artist problem, and the moms underneath it kept the ideas coming.

Credit: @thriving_out_of_spite, @norcalcaro and @sksargeant via Threads

One mom’s solution doubled as entertainment.

(If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.)

Toddler palates are a moving target. The food they inhaled one day is suddenly disgusting the next. A couple of moms found that a little creative branding goes a long way, at the table and beyond.

Brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

When a meltdown hits, plenty of moms agreed the first move is regulating yourself. Toddlers take their emotional cues from us, so the calmer we stay, the faster they come back down.

From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

That sniff trick is a cousin of the viral “Jessica” trick, where a parent interrupts a meltdown by calmly calling for someone who isn’t there. Pediatrician Dr. Madison Szar told Motherly that “What’s that smell?” works just as well, since the surprise is what breaks the loop. Bonus points for the deep breaths.

And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.

Then there are the white lies. One bedtime fib stood out as particularly clever.

Having raised two kids, one in college and one in high school, I can attest that I lied to them. A lot. The car won’t start unless you’re buckled. It’s against the law to take your shoes off in the store. The toy store is closing, so we have to leave now. I promise you they are both 100% trustworthy, honest people.

When I was a new mom, just 21 and wildly out of my depth, I had a mentor with a toddler of her own. A yoga teacher who became a mom in her early 40s, she was a free spirit who didn’t mother through the lens of anyone else’s scrutiny. It was wild and refreshing.

She was willing to be inconvenienced so her son could explore and held firm when exploring teetered toward danger. She also leaned into the absurdity. At one point she’d somehow acquired a shopping cart, and when her son got grumpy, she’d load him in with a rug, some toys and their cat (I’m not kidding) and march around the neighborhood with the dog following behind.

Toddlers are ridiculous, and we all know it. Sometimes you have to meet the moment with the same.

The Autoscooper 12 is the newest self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot. The US company was founded in Portland, Oregon, in 2023. Add some clumping bentonite-clay litter and presto! Being naturally curious and experienced automatic litter box users, my cats wasted no time becoming intimately familiar with their shiny new toilet, and the AutoScooper 12 is even quieter than the one I already have! The Sabah lives in the sweet spot between a loafer and a slipper, without looking much like either. Handmade in Turkey, the Blackout version pairs soft black leather with hand stitching, a leather insole that shapes to his foot, and a replaceable rubber outsole. Wear it with trousers, shorts or whatever passes for his weekend uniform. It's the sort of relaxed, distinctive shoe you notice precisely because it isn't trying so hard.

Most headphones are anonymous plastic. Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro looks like someone actually thought about the design. Behind the striking shell are three drivers, adaptive noise cancellation, and tuning developed with Metropolis Studios. Real buttons and dials mean less fumbling at the earcups, while the battery runs up to 68 hours with noise cancellation off. For a dad who's spent enough time listening to other people's playlists, here's a way back to his own.

It has a tuning dial. An actual dial. Tivoli's Model One is a gorgeous antidote to the idea that every piece of technology needs an app and a setup tutorial. The wood cabinet, simple knobs, and traditional AM/FM radio make it a pleasure to use, while Bluetooth is there when he wants to stream something. Set it on a desk or bookshelf. Turn it on. Listen. Remember when that was all it took?

Marshall's Minor IV earbuds have a little of the brand's old-school amplifier swagger, minus the equipment truck. The black-and-gold finish is sharp, the angled design is made for a comfortable fit, and touch controls handle music and calls. Battery life runs up to seven hours per charge and more than 30 with the case. They're water-resistant, too. A solid upgrade for the dad who still cares what comes through his headphones, even if he now listens at a more reasonable volume.

If he has opinions about beans, water temperature, and extraction times, he needs a grinder that can keep up. Fellow's Opus 2 handles everything from espresso to cold brew, with fine grind adjustments and 48-millimeter conical burrs. Anti-static technology cuts down on the mess, and magnetic catch cups make switching methods simple. The sleek profile doesn't hurt. But the point isn't the countertop aesthetic. It's better coffee before any guests start asking where their shoes are.

This year’s Booker prize winner is a dystopian sci-fi satire that takes place up and down the British coast. It’s not exactly a beach read, but a novel that is a perfectly odd reflection of our perfectly strange times.

A slab of teak isn't an obvious gift until you see this one. Sonder LA's Bradbury board has three compartments for chopped ingredients or a serious cheese spread. Turn it over and a deep groove catches up to 4.5 ounces of carving juices, saving the counter from the aftermath of Sunday dinner. Heavy, handsome, and useful enough to leave out all the time. It's the cutting board version of buying one good thing instead of three mediocre ones.

Smithey's cast-iron chef skillet looks like something a grandparent might have handed down, except this one comes ready to start its own history. The polished interior develops seasoning over time, the curved sides make tossing food easier, and the weight holds heat beautifully for searing. It's made in South Carolina and looks good enough to bring straight to the table. For the dad who finds chopping onions therapeutic and considers a well-seasoned pan a point of pride.

A drawer full of knives is no substitute for one excellent one. Made In's 8-inch chef knife is forged in Thiers, France, by a fifth-generation bladesmith, with a full-tang construction that gives it balance and control. It can mince herbs, chop vegetables, and tackle the Sunday roast without switching tools. The best part is how often he'll use it. Unlike most expensive kitchen gifts, this won't spend its life on display.

Finding a night when everyone's free is now the hardest part of poker. Mark & Graham takes care of everything else: two decks of cards, 100 chips, and a pebbled-leather case lined in suede. It's compact enough to put away but handsome enough not to. Add a monogram if he likes that sort of thing. Then put an evening on the calendar and let him spend a few hours with people who don't need help finding their cleats.

No sprawling backyard? No problem. Solo Stove's Mesa XL brings a real flame to a compact tabletop fire pit, with an airflow system that helps keep smoke down. The stainless-steel body looks good on a patio, and the setup is simple enough for an impromptu evening outside. Roast marshmallows with the kids or pull up chairs after bedtime. It's a small fire with an outsized ability to make an ordinary Tuesday feel like something else.

The mind of the famous neurologist Oliver Sacks was like no other. His letters show his thoughts in full light — restless, deep, and full of love and wisdom. Think of this book as competency porn — a counter to the daily doomscrolling.

Chess is a wonderful game, provided you enjoy being intellectually humiliated by a 12-year-old. This smart chessboard might help him even the odds. Built-in sensors track every move, while LED lights suggest what to do next, and AI-powered coaching helps players improve without enduring another smug lecture about strategy. Connect it to Chess.com or Lichess to challenge opponents around the world, play against the computer, or settle a family rivalry the old-fashioned way.

A puffer jacket for your neck sounds ridiculous until the temperature drops. Cotopaxi's Fuego Down Scarf delivers the warmth of an insulated jacket in a lightweight, packable scarf, with responsibly sourced down, a water-resistant recycled nylon shell, and bold color-blocked stripes. A pull-through slit keeps it securely in place, while pockets at either end give Dad somewhere to warm his hands when gloves aren't enough.

A leisurely hike is one thing. Scrambling up a rocky trail and navigating a steep descent is another. Leki's Makalu Cork Lite trekking poles give Dad some extra stability when the terrain gets tricky, without weighing him down. Made from lightweight aluminum, each pole weighs less than 9 ounces and has an ergonomic cork grip that absorbs moisture and gradually conforms to his hand. Adjustable locking mechanisms make it easy to change the length on the go, while carbide tips provide traction on uneven ground. They telescope down for packing, too.

The nightstand looks like a cable graveyard. Anker's MagStand gives it a chance at redemption, charging three devices with a magnetic pad for compatible iPhones, a retractable USB-C cable, and another USB-C port. A small display shows charging status and other information, while a quieter overnight mode suits a bedroom. It's the sort of unglamorous upgrade that feels extremely glamorous the first time he reaches for a fully charged phone and doesn't pull a nest of wires off the table.

For the Formula 1 dad with extremely confident opinions about tire strategy. Logitech's McLaren racing bundle pairs an F1-style wheel with direct-drive force feedback, so the steering pushes back as traction and cornering forces change in the game. It's far closer to a simulator than a standard controller, and requires the space and enthusiasm to match. A serious indulgence, yes. But probably less expensive than any other way of letting him pretend he's on the grid.

At some point in your parenting adventures, whether you like it or not, you will have to face the trials and tribulations of what it means to be a teenager. This book deeply, and sometimes even profoundly, explores just this, with equal parts science and storytelling, it might not help you truly prepare for your little one to hit their pubescence, but it will give you empathy and maybe even a bit of appreciation.

Keys jangle, scratch phones, and vanish precisely when everyone is late. Orbitkey stacks three to seven of them inside a slim leather organizer, then adds a tracker that works with Apple Find My or Google Find Hub on compatible devices. It takes less room in a pocket and looks considerably better than a bulky ring. Not the showiest gift here. Possibly the one he'll use most often.

Remember when listening to music meant putting on an album and actually listening to the whole thing? The Retradisc CD player brings back that pleasure, minus the tangled headphone cords. Its transparent case lets Dad watch his CDs spin, while Bluetooth connectivity lets him pair it with wireless headphones or speakers. There's also a traditional headphone jack, anti-skip protection, and a rechargeable battery.

Some dads count steps. Others count elevation gain. Garmin's Enduro 4 is for the second group, with trail maps, endurance metrics, stamina tracking, and more than 100 activity profiles. Its solar-assisted battery can last up to 90 days in smartwatch mode under Garmin's specified sunlight conditions, which makes it especially useful on long trips. It's overkill for walking the dog. For someone planning his next ultramarathon before finishing the last one, that's the appeal.

Klipsch's The Nines II are some of the most drool-worthy bookshelf speakers out there. With DTS:X support and an 8-inch cerametallic woofer, dedicated analog input, and a built-in phono stage, Klipsch is for vinyl lovers. The new red oak veneer with a white is our pick because, well, look at it.

He tracks workouts, sleep, and maybe his resting heart rate. Why stop at weight? Withings' BodyScan 2 measures composition by body region, tracks muscle and fat mass, and offers cardiovascular metrics including a six-lead ECG and vascular age estimates. Results appear on a screen built into the handle. Some advanced analysis requires a subscription, and it's not a replacement for a doctor. Buy it for the data enthusiast who actually wants this information, not as a hint that somebody should get in shape.

The fleece vest has spent far too long being associated with finance bros who say things like “let's circle back.” It's time to reclaim it. The North Face's Glacier Vest is lightweight, warm, and made entirely from recycled polyester fleece. It's the ideal extra layer for chilly morning walks, weekend hikes, or an office where someone has apparently mistaken the thermostat for a refrigerator dial.

Because exercise equipment has a way of proliferating and is generally ugly, at-home workouts tend to require a sacrifice of one kind or another. The possible lone exception is the rowing machine: Rowing works 86 percent of the body’s muscles and can be as cardio-intense (or mellow) as you like, while improving joint flexibility. One of the newest and sleekest rowing machines, the Ergatta uses actual water resistance, which makes it as effective as it is quiet (as well as cool-looking, with its transparent reservoir). It’s got all the fitness potential of a traditional rowing machine, but packaged with cutting-edge, immersive technology (a reasonable $29/month) that keeps monotony at bay. The jewel in the crown, though, is its design: Handmade of cherry wood, it's the farthest thing from an eyesore, and it can be folded up and stowed away, so it works in even the tiniest of homes.

Just looking at this hammock drops your diastolic blood pressure. String this version up between two trees, or on a stand, and the generous 55-by-82-inch hammock will cradle him with an open back that prevents sweating in the summer heat. The cord is as soft as cotton, but the synthetic blend inhibits discoloration in the sun, is anti-microbial, and easy to clean with soap and water when the kids spill watermelon on it.

Sure, you can find a dozen pricey, aesthetically arresting turntables out there, but for the man who actually listens to his records, you can't beat AudioTechnica. The biggest upgrade for a vinyl spin is found in the manual turntable and the seemingly no-frills AT-LPW30 puts all the focus on great sound and proper listening experience.

He may be shaving in a hurry, but the products don't have to feel like a compromise. Le Labo pairs a rich shaving cream with a soothing after-shave balm in minimalist aluminum tubes. Bergamot, lavender, violet, and tonka bean give the set a distinctive scent without the usual blast of drugstore aftershave. It turns a boring morning task into something a little more civilized. No 10-step ritual required.

A beautiful new edition of William Gibson's seminal 1984 cyberpunk novel. Illustrated throughout by Anna Mill, with a handsome slipcase.

Aventus is not a subtle little stocking stuffer. It's Creed's big, unapologetically luxurious fragrance, with fresh bergamot and blackcurrant giving way to pineapple, pink pepper, and smoky birch. The mix feels rich without veering into syrupy. Yes, the price is extravagant. That's rather the point. For a dad who's particular about fragrance and rarely buys the expensive bottle for himself, this is a proper splurge.

If the household has a snorer, a restless sleeper, or a neighbor who enjoys late-night construction projects, these might be the most welcome gift of the season. Ozlo's Sleepbuds 2 sit low in the ear, including for side sleepers, and play sleep sounds to help mask noise. They can also stream music or podcasts, with up to 14 hours of battery life and a private in-ear alarm. The case monitors bedroom conditions, too. They can't make anyone sleep later. They might make the hours he gets a little quieter.

Dad's face has been through a lot. Early mornings, late nights, questionable sleep, and possibly decades of washing it with whatever soap happens to be in the shower. It deserves better. Caldera + Lab's The Regimen gives him a proper skin care routine without requiring a degree in dermatology. The four-piece set includes a gentle exfoliating cleanser, a botanical serum, a daily moisturizer, and an eye treatment designed to tackle the appearance of puffiness and dark circles.

Some people throw out a broken gadget. Others want to see exactly what's gone wrong inside. iFixit's Mako kit is for the latter, with 64 precision bits for laptops, game consoles, phones, and the obscure screws that defeat an ordinary screwdriver. The aluminum driver has a magnetic socket and swivel top; the case keeps everything from scattering across the table. A small, deeply satisfying gift for the dad who believes almost anything deserves one attempt at repair.

The moment you become a dad, people start assuming you can fix things. Leatherman's Wingman won't supply the expertise, but it gives him 14 ways to look prepared. Spring-action pliers, scissors, screwdrivers, wire cutters, a blade, and a package opener all fold into one pocketable tool. The knife opens with one hand and the 25-year warranty suggests it's meant to stick around. One of those gifts he'll reach for long after the holidays are forgotten.

Flat-pack furniture has destroyed more relationships than anyone cares to admit. Hoto's PivotDrive won't save a marriage, but it might prevent an argument over a bookshelf. This sleek cordless screwdriver has a head that pivots 90 degrees, with four locking positions to reach screws buried in tight corners and awkward spaces. Five torque settings, two speeds, and 16 interchangeable bits handle everything from furniture assembly to minor household repairs. It's a clever upgrade for the guy who enjoys fixing things almost as much as complaining about how badly they were designed.

#7926. 9 Frozen Puff Pastry Desserts That Only Look High Effort

These treats bring the bakery-worthy wow factor without the professional-level effort.

There are few kitchen shortcuts I love more than keeping a box of puff pastry in the freezer. It’s the secret weapon behind so many desserts that look like they came from a fancy bakery, even when you barely had to lift a finger to make them. We’re talking flaky layers, pretty little twists, golden-brown pastries and impressive-looking tarts, all without the hassle of cutting cold butter into flour while simultaneously pouring in ice water (IYKYK).

If Nutella is your love language, these Nutella puff pastries from A Sweet Thyme need to be on your baking list. Store-bought puff pastry gets brushed with melted butter, spread with Nutella, and sprinkled with ground hazelnuts before being folded, sliced, and twisted into pretty little pastries. They bake up golden and flaky in just 12 to 15 minutes, making them look like something you’d pick up at a European bakery.

You don’t need a deep fryer or a trip to your favorite churro stand to get that cinnamon-sugar goodness. Princess Pinky Girl’s churro twists use just three ingredients — puff pastry, melted butter, and cinnamon sugar — to bring this dream dessert to the table. The whole recipe takes about 15 minutes, which means you can have a batch ready before your guests even finish their first cup of coffee.

If you’re looking for a dessert that doubles as a centerpiece, this strawberry puff pastry snowflake from Sugarbird Cakery & Floral is a showstopper. Despite its impressive appearance, it only requires three sheets of puff pastry, strawberry jam, melted butter, cinnamon sugar, and an egg wash. The finished snowflake is almost too pretty to eat. Almost.

These cherry and cream cheese turnovers from Averie Cooks have serious bakery case energy, but they’re surprisingly simple to make at home. Flaky puff pastry is cut into squares and filled with cream cheese and cherry preserves before being folded into little triangles, brushed with egg wash, and sprinkled with coarse sugar. Don’t skip the best part: a sweet vanilla cream cheese glaze drizzled over the top.

Cinnamon rolls are always a good idea, but making them from scratch can turn into an all-morning project. Barefoot in the Pines’ puff pastry cinnamon rolls give you all the buttery, cinnamon-sugary goodness without the yeast, rising, waiting, and margin for error. They’re especially good for holiday mornings when you want something homemade without adding another complicated recipe to your to-do list.

This caramelized pear tart from Brown Eyed Baker looks like something you’d order at a fancy restaurant, but the secret is just a sheet of store-bought puff pastry. Pear slices are mixed with a homemade caramel sauce in a skillet, topped with puff pastry and baked until golden. Once it’s finished, you flip the tart over to reveal the beautifully caramelized pears underneath. Don’t forget a scoop of vanilla ice cream for serving!

If you love a classic apple dessert but don’t want to fuss with homemade pie crust, consider Well Plated’s upside-down apple tart. Apple slices are arranged over butter, honey, brown sugar, and cinnamon, then covered with a sheet of puff pastry and baked until everything is golden and bubbling. Once you flip it over, the apples are beautifully arranged on top, creating a beautiful tart that looks far more complicated than it actually is — and no one has to know it took just a few minutes to prep.

These cream cheese Danishes from Princess Pinky Girl use puff pastry to create a flaky base for a sweet filling made with cream cheese, maple syrup, yogurt, vanilla, and a touch of lemon juice. They’re perfect for a holiday brunch, dessert table, or anytime you want something that looks like it came straight from a professional bakery.

It seems with the help of a frozen puff pastry, even those of us with nothing left to give can whip up an impressive dessert in no time.

#7925. This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

Don’t panic if your Christmas cactus isn’t flowering yet because this quick pro growers’ hack can help kickstart the process, bringing beautiful blooms in time for the big day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective. It’s so disappointing when a Schlumbergera isn’t showing even the smallest pinpricks of colored buds on its stem ends by late fall, especially if you’ve been diligently delivering all the care your Christmas cactus needs in November. But by shifting your stubborn plant into survival mode, you can kickstart its bloom cycle. And guess what? All you need is a banana and a plastic bag.

Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones. This causes the plants to stop growing green leaf segments and switch to developing flowerbuds. And you can use the exact same idea with the natural chemicals a ripe banana releases if your Christmas cactus isn't blooming yet.

We all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast. That’s down to the ethylene it emits, a natural hormone that plants release when nearing the end of their life cycle. So, by trapping ethylene around your Christmas cactus for a short time, you can trick the plant into thinking it’s under extreme threat, which triggers it to develop flowers as a last-ditch survival effort to preserve its genetics via seed production. Clever, huh?

Highly ripe bananas that have brown spots or are turning brown emit the highest levels of ethylene. You only need to use the peel: though the whole fruit produces ethylene gas, the soft, sweet flesh of a banana is a magnet for fruit flies and fungus gnats and adds too much moisture to the little greenhouse you’re about to create.

Excess moisture will quickly evaporate from the inner surface of the peel, further reducing humidity and any risk of pests or disease.

Now stand your Christmas cactus, still in its container, on a plate or big plant saucer and lay the banana peel alongside the pot base. It’s important that the peel doesn’t touch the leaf segments or soil as this risks transferring mold or fungal spores.

Pull a clear plastic bag down over the plant, plate and banana peel, and tuck or tie under the plate to seal. If the bag is flimsy and falls onto the stems, use chopsticks or skewers poked into the soil to create a frame so there's no direction contact between plant and plastic.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It’s important the bag is clear as an opaque bag is likely to take the stress a step too far and your plant may drop leaf segments instead of developing buds. It also means you can keep a close eye on your plant through the process. A clear unscented trash bag like this from Amazon is ideal as it's plenty big enough to make fashioning your mini-greenhouse easy.

Now your Christmas cactus is in its little greenhouse, it’ll quickly overheat if it’s hit by the sun’s rays so find it a spot in a bright room but out of direct sunlight.

The optimum amount of time to leave your Schlumbergera in its ethylene tank is exactly 2 days and 2 nights. This gives the gas plenty of time to chemically shock the plant and trigger bud development, without damaging the plant or giving mold a chance to develop in the restricted air circulation.

While professional growers use incredibly precise parts-per-million doses of synthetic chemicals, you can’t tell exactly how much ethylene your chosen banana is emitting. So, keep an eye on your Christmas cactus and if at any point the plant looks like it’s struggling or there’s the slightest sign of mold, remove the bag straight away. Don’t be tempted to leave the bag on any longer than 48 hours as too much ethylene can harm bud development.

Carefully take off the plastic bag, discard the peel and place your plant in the spot where you want it to flower, being sure to avoid these Christmas cactus disaster zones. After a week or so, you should see pinhead-sized bumps starting to form on the leaf segment tips and by two weeks, they should be clearly visible.

It’s vital you check your plant hasn’t already begun developing buds before trying this trick. Inspect leaf tips under a bright light – or use a cheap magnifying glass with LED light like this from Amazon – to look for any bumps beginning to form right on the tips of the leaf segments. These may be tiny so gently feel for them with a fingertip, too. If your Schlumbergera has pink or red flowers these little bumps will be bright but if your plant blooms white they may be green and harder to spot.

If you’re in any doubt, wait a week and see if those bumps get any bigger. While using ethylene from ripe banana peel is a very effective way to get a Christmas cactus to flower, this hormone shock can also cause existing buds to stall if the process has already begun.

If this pro growers' trick doesn’t work, there’s likely an underlying reason why your Christmas cactus isn't flowering, that’s overriding the plant’s system.

The banana bag trick is well worth trying if your Christmas cactus doesn’t have buds yet, and you still just have enough time to trigger your plant into producing flowers for the holidays. Next year, be sure to use the black-out hack that tricks your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time, and you won’t have to worry!

#7924. How to thank school support staff this American Education Week (Hint: It’s not a mug)

The school staff our kids love most are often the ones paid the least. Here’s how to thank them during American Education Week.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 16, 2026

My son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse. She was warm and welcoming, always quick with a comforting hug. More importantly, she had the best Band-Aids in the building, and she wasn’t stingy about giving them out.  A scraped knee got one. So did a paper cut, and even some invisible injuries, too. She knew when a kid headed to see her, it wasn’t necessarily about needing that Band-Aid.

That nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did. There were kids who came to her office with a belly ache that wasn’t a stomach bug, but because they hadn’t had breakfast, and possibly dinner either. There were kids who could barely stay awake in class because they’d spent the night in a car instead of a bed. She met those kids with the same warmth she gave my Band-Aid collector, and I’m certain she kept a stash of snacks in her desk for those visits in particular.

People like her have a name in education circles. They’re education support professionals, or ESPs, and they include school nurses, cafeteria workers, bus drivers, security staff, paraeducators, technical personnel, custodians, skilled trade workers, and front office staff. Ask kids about their favorite grown-up at school, and there’s a decent chance the answer is one of them.

The people our kids adore are often the people schools pay the least. Nearly 32% of full-time ESPs earn less than $25,000 a year, according to the National Education Association, and on average, they’re paid below a living wage in all 50 states.

That’s not a livable wage in most areas. “Our wages are so low, we are forced to have two or three jobs,” paraeducator Yahaira Rodriguez told NEA Today. The nurse who stays late with a hungry kid may be heading to a second job after school, eating dinner in the car on the way. That’s a long day for someone whose job is to take care of everyone else’s kids. It also makes it hard to stay in the job. Before the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported trouble filling at least one non-teaching position, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That means the kids who rely on them the most are the ones who lose out when they leave or the positions can’t be filled.

The NEA ESP Bill of Rights lays out what these professionals need to stay in the jobs our kids depend on. Developed by ESPs themselves, it asks for pay that covers the bills without a second job, health care they can afford and a workplace ‘free of violence, including physical, verbal, and emotional abuse.’ It’s a practical document about what it takes to keep these jobs filled. The full list includes:

Since the movement began, 18 states have launched ESP Bill of Rights campaigns, according to NEA.

American Education Week runs November 16 to 20, 2026, and this year NEA is using it to honor education support staff. Here are a few ways to show up for the people who show up for our kids:

Our kids won’t remember most of what happened at school, but they’ll remember who was kind to them there. For a lot of them, that’s a nurse, a cafeteria staff or a bus driver doing the job on less than a living wage. Sign the ESP Bill of Rights pledge and help them stay.

#7923. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

#7920. The Common Flea Pill Preventing New World Screwworm

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

For many cat parents, the brand Capstar might ring a bell. This small, fast-acting tablet has long been used to kill adult fleas on cats and dogs. Now, the active ingredient in Capstar, nitenpyram, is being given an important new role: treating and preventing New World screwworm.

On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA for nitenpyram tablets, allowing the common flea tablet to be used off-label for the prevention and treatment of New World screwworm infestations in cats, kittens, dogs, and puppies.

Why does this matter? Because until now, prevention was the missing piece when it came to drug options for dogs and cats. This new authorization helps fill that gap, giving veterinarians another tool in the toolbox while the larger fight against New World screwworm continues.

First things first: despite the rather dramatic name, New World screwworm is not a worm at all. It is a fly: Cochliomyia hominivorax. The âwormâ part of the name comes from the larvae, or maggot, of this fly. And unfortunately, this is one fly that definitely deserves our attention.

The trouble starts when a female fly finds a suitable place to lay her eggs, usually in or around a wound. She can also target other vulnerable areas, including the eyes, nose, mouth, and other mucous membranes. Once those eggs hatch, the larvae get to work, and this is where the screwworm becomes particularly nasty.

These aren't the disgusting but harmless little maggots that make themselves at home in overflowing trash cans or rotting food. Screwworm larvae feed on living tissue, burrowing deep into the affected area, feeding as they grow. Before long, a wound that looks small on the outside has become a much bigger problem underneath. An infestation can cause extensive tissue damage and, without prompt treatment, can even be life-threatening.

New World screwworm has been detected in the United States, while Mexico and other countries in the region continue to deal with the parasite. USDA is maintaining surveillance and response efforts, including in Texas, where âzones of infestationâ have been established.

The concern goes well beyond individual animals. Screwworm can have a serious economic impact on livestock production because affected animals may lose weight, require treatment and extra care, or die. During a 1976 outbreak in Texas, producers spent an estimated $132.1 million dealing with the pest, equivalent to about $740 million in 2024 dollars. More recently, the disruption to live cattle exports from Mexico has been estimated to have cost that country's livestock sector around $1.8 billion.

This is why so much effort is going into keeping this fly from spreading. This is about animal health, but it is also about protecting our entire food production system.

And no, the strategy is not simply âfind the bugs and squish them.â Controlling screwworm takes a much bigger effort. Authorities are using surveillance, movement controls, trapping, and other measures, along with one particularly interesting tool: releasing sterile flies.

The idea is surprisingly simple. Sterile male flies are released into affected areas, where they compete with fertile males for mates. When a sterile male mates with a female, she does not produce viable offspring. Over time, this can cripple the wild screwworm population.

The good news is that this isn't something every cat owner needs to panic about. Where a cat lives, where it travels, and whether it spends time in an area where screwworm is present all make a difference. For cats traveling to or returning from affected areas, it's worth being a little more careful.

With screwworm, the goal is to understand the risk before the exposure happens and, whenever possible, st ay one step ahead of the fly. When you consider that cats are experts at hiding things, including small wounds, a puncture, scratch, or other break in the skin can be easy to miss under all that fur, especially in an outdoor cat.

A wound can become an invitation for a female screwworm fly to lay her eggs, and the larvae that hatch will feed on living tissue. Cats infested with screwworm larvae have wounds that aren't healing normally, visible maggots, an unusual odor, or discharge. In any situation, these signs warrant veterinary attention. If you happen to live near or have traveled to an area where the New World screwworm has been detected, be sure to mention it to your vet.

Not necessarily. This does not mean Capstar should suddenly become part of every cat's routine parasite prevention. As a flea treatment, it is particularly effective at killing adult fleas quickly, but doesnât provide long-term flea control.

A cat living indoors in an area where screwworm isn't present is in a very different situation from a cat traveling to an affected region or spending time outdoors there. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether your cat's particular situation calls for the medication.

In the case of screwworm, Capstar is used according to the Emergency Use Authorization, not the FDA-approved standard use. There are specific instructions for when and how it should be given.

If you're traveling with your cat to an area where screwworm has been identified, or returning from one, talk with your veterinarian before you go. International travel can also come with health certificates, inspections, and other paperwork, and the requirements vary depending on the country you're entering or passing through. Some documents must be completed within a specific window before travel, so don't leave the paperwork until the last minute.

For most cats, New World screwworm is not something to worry about every day. But for cats living in or traveling to affected areas, knowing the risk, knowing that preventive options are available, and knowing what to look for can make a real difference. Itâs also great to know that those options include a product that has been safely used in cats for decades.

The takeaway isn't that every cat needs Capstar, but when a parasite like screwworm becomes a concern, having a preventive option available can make it easier to protect cats that are actually at risk.

And when a parasite feeds on living tissue, âbetter safe than sorryâ is a pretty good philosophy.

#7919. E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A new JAMA study shows e-bike injuries in kids climbing quarter after quarter. Two pediatric physicians break down who’s ready to ride, which bikes and helmets to choose and when a crash means a trip to the ER.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 19, 2026

E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

“It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt says. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

Timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he says. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”

In the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt says, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

A child is ready, Natt says, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt says, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

Timmons says a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons says fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

After the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt says. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

Any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons says. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

Watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons says. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

If the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons says, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

“These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt says. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”

That's right; instead of bringing an evergreen indoors, many people celebrate the season beneath a spectacular flowering tree covered in brilliant red blooms. Meet the New Zealand Christmas Tree, also known as the pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). This extraordinary evergreen puts on one of the most eye-catching floral displays of summer, transforming coastlines and gardens with masses of vibrant crimson flowers.

And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...

Native to New Zealand, the pōhutukawa has earned its festive nickname thanks to its spectacular flowering season, which coincides with Christmas in the Southern Hemisphere. Because, while much of the northern hemisphere is welcoming winter with bare branches and chilly temperatures, New Zealand is enjoying the height of summer... and that's when this remarkable tree really comes into its own.

Rather than having conventional petals, its unmistakable flowers look just like fluffy red brushes (which pollinators love). And, against the tree's glossy green leaves, the effect is nothing short of spectacular.

A post shared by Hahana (@hahana_official)

Although it can reach around 65 feet tall in its natural habitat, younger New Zealand Christmas trees can be grown from seed in large containers (although they need plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil and protection from frost).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

For US gardeners, growing one outdoors will generally be limited to warmer and frost-free USDA Zones, so it isn't necessarily a practical choice for everyone. Luckily, though, there are other flowering evergreens that can deliver a similarly spectacular effect...

If it's the striking crimson display of the pōhutukawa that catches your eye, bottlebrush is perhaps the closest alternative when it comes to finding a flowering evergreen that might serve well as a Christmas tree. Especially as its bright red blooms have plenty in common with the Kiwi native.

Depending on the variety and climate, bottlebrush (available at Walmart) can flower from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. Many varieties are evergreen and container-friendly, too, although they prefer a sunny position and well-drained soil.

For gardeners who love the idea of a flowering Christmas tree, but prefer something with more traditional-looking blooms, southern magnolia is a beautiful option, as its enormous (and fabulously fragranced) flowers can measure up to 12 inches across.

While it doesn't have the bright red flowers of the pōhutukawa, it shares some of its most appealing qualities: year-round evergreen foliage, a substantial tree-like presence and an impressive summer floral display. For smaller spaces, consider a compact cultivar such as this 'Little Gem' from Expert Gardener. It has a naturally narrower growth habit than many full-sized southern magnolias, making it a more manageable choice for smaller gardens.

It can also be grown in a large container so long as you treat it to sufficient room, good drainage and consistent moisture.

If fragrance is just as important as appearance, gardenia is another gorgeous Christmas tree alternative thanks to its deep-green foliage and exquisite white flowers.

Oh sure, their blooms may be smaller than those of the southern magnolia, but they more than make up for it with their intoxicating perfume. And, as they don't naturally grow into large trees, standard-trained gardenias can make particularly attractive container garden options; generally best suited to warmer USDA growing zones, growing them in pots makes it easier to protect them from cold weather.

Something like the Frost Proof Gardenia from Nature Hills is happily able to handle temperatures down to 0-10°F, too!

The New Zealand Christmas Tree is a wonderful reminder that evergreens don't have to be all about foliage; indeed, some of the most spectacular trees and shrubs combine year-round greenery with extraordinary seasonal flowers.

Whether you choose the fiery red blooms of bottlebrush, the impressive flowers of southern magnolia or the beautiful fragrance of gardenia, there's no shortage of ways to bring that flowering-evergreen look into your own garden. And who knows? You might even find yourself looking at your Christmas tree traditions a little differently as a result...

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7916. Who’s a Scaredy Cat? Keeping Cats Safe This Halloween

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting new people.

The biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

Keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most important Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

With trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

Carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

It can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

Cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

However, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.
