Fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

Fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

This year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

Many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

It’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

Instead of endlessly raking, run a mulching mower, like this Greenworks model, over the grass as needed, chopping up the leaves when you see light to moderate coverage. Another option is to remove some of a thick layer of leaves for use in compost or as a mulch in beds. Don’t worry about removing every last leaf before winter.

Fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A simple rain gauge, such as this easy-to-read JMBay model from Amazon, can help you keep track of rainfall. Keep an eye on the soil and rain and decide when the grass could use a deep drink rather than sticking with a strict schedule.

Of course, there are exceptions. If you have seeded parts of the lawn or installed new sod before winter, these areas should be watered regularly right up until the ground freezes.

At some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but plan to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

Keep mowing to the recommended height for your type of grass until the final cut. A tool like the Oregon Deck Leveling Gauge from Amazon can help you check your mower's cutting height and ensure an even cut.

As growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

Bagging all of your healthy grass clippings is unnecessary. It’s also a highly labor-intensive chore. Don’t waste your time, energy, or back on this one. Finely chopped grass decomposes quickly and adds nutrients to the soil. And, contrary to popular belief, grass clippings left on the ground do not contribute to thatch buildup.

Instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer big clumps you'll get.

Managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

Instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

Fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

Cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

Your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

Instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

As you plan fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.

#7902. The Secret to National Happiness is More Cats…or is it?

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats = happiness. Itâs an equation that neither cat lovers nor the cats themselves will find surprising, but itâs not something you expect to be evaluated, let alone proven, through scientific research. In a recent correlational study of subjective well-being across 93 countries, researchers examined the relationship between cat density, exposure to Toxoplasma gondii, socioeconomic status, and national happiness, with interesting results.

According to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context. The key word in this study is correlational. Researchers have not discovered that happiness levels are the result of larger feline populations â ie, a causal relationship â only that there is a notable connection between countries reporting higher numbers of pet cats and those ranked highest on the World Population Reviewâs 2025 report on the Happiest Countries in the World.

So before you trade your antidepressant prescription for a kitten, there are a few things worth understanding.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood

The researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

Interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

The study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

We know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. They somehow have the ability to draw a smile on our face without saying a single word, simply by lying on our lap or sitting beside us after a difficult day. Emotional support comes in many forms, and cats seem to know just the right way to make us feel happier, calmer, and more at ease.

But personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

Hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

In other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

Financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are important too.

This wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

Countries with more people showing signs of a recent infection tended to have lower happiness scores. To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Neither provides a perfect timeline of when the infection occurred.

Thereâs another important detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Differences in hygiene, food safety, healthcare access, and economic circumstances could influence both infection rates and well-being. After all, health and happiness are difficult to separate from the conditions we live in. Ask anyone who cannot turn on a tap and count on clean, safe water. A parasite may be part of the picture, but so are the everyday resources that help us stay healthy, feel secure, and simply have an easier and more comfortable day-to-day.

T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

Pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

Cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. A cat who retreats, flattens their ears, or flicks their tail may be asking for space. Ignoring those signs because a human wants affection isn't bonding; it's treating a living, breathing creature like a plush toy.

Good care means respecting those boundaries. Hiding places, elevated resting spots, predictable routines, interactive play, and regular veterinary care all help support feline well-being. Changes in behavior often signal pain or illness, so they deserve attention rather than an automatic label of âbad behavior.â

And no, not every cat wants to be carried around like a furry handbag. Some barely tolerate being looked at when they're minding their own business. That's not a character flaw. It's a cat making its position very clear.

The study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

For cat families, the practical health advice is simple: litter box hygiene is paramount. Scoop the poop daily, since T. gondii oocysts generally need one to five days after being shed to become infectious. Wash your hands after handling litter, wear gloves while gardening, cook meat thoroughly, and make sure you wash and disinfect fruits and veggies before eating.

Pregnant women and those with a weak immune system should consult their doctor about appropriate precautions. During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

Ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

A familiar purr, a gentle head bump, or a cat choosing your lap to nap in can brighten an ordinary afternoon and put a smile on anyoneâs face. The 3 a.m. bedroom sprints and hairballs left over the Persian rug, however, remain entirely separate research questions!

#7901. School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

The menu in your child’s cafeteria isn’t set by chance. It’s the result of a multi-year federal process, and you can weigh in on how it changes.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 23, 2026

This article is sponsored by Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI). Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an update, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are currently implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

The USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

The USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI,  “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”

This group of hand-picked authors created a new “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

As in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

However, it’s also likely the new proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources).  For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

The best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

The regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

#7899. So You Think You Have Insomnia. What Now?

Even if you’re not comfortable taking medication, there are other treatment options out there.

When you’re a parent, it’s sometimes hard to tell what is a normal amount of tired and what’s an unhealthy level of exhaustion. Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings, it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep, there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers, board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

“If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” says Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

“Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up too early, or just having really poor, unrefreshing sleep. There are no guidelines on how long it takes you to fall asleep or how long you’re awake in the middle of the night, but you have to be unhappy with it at least three times a week for at least three months for it to meet full criteria for chronic insomnia,” Meers explains.

If you’ve noticed your husband starts snoring within seconds of his head hitting the pillow, you’re not alone. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which experts have chalked up to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the bulk of the mental load in the family.

“One of the biggest reasons we think for this is that as women, we cycle through our monthly menstrual cycle, and the dynamics and the changing of those hormones set us up to have more disrupted and more fragmented sleep at certain times of the cycle versus other times,” says Meers.

“Also, we have a lot of role strain as women. We carry a lot of caretaking activities and responsibilities, especially in women who are in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, who are trying to take care of everyone and have a career and be productive and make sure that we’re taking care of our kids the way we value or give them the life we want them to live. Stress directly impacts insomnia and our ability to sleep. So it really becomes this negative feedback cycle.”

You could definitely start by scheduling an appointment with your primary care doctor, if you have one. However, surveys show the average doctor only receives about 2.5 hours of education on sleep during medical school. Depending on your concerns and potential causes of your sleeplessness, they might refer you to a sleep medicine physician, a neurologist, a psychiatrist, or a sleep psychologist.

You may have never heard of sleep psychologists like Meers before, but they are specifically trained in the dynamics of sleep and sussing out underlying medical causes of insomnia (like sleep apnea) versus behavioral causes.

“I talk to a lot of primary care physicians. A lot of times they feel constrained to just give medications, nor do they have the time to really assess what’s going on because they have just so much to do in such a short amount of time,” Meers says. “So if you have the ability to see a sleep specialist like me who's a psychologist, I recommend starting there. And then if this is a medical issue, we are really good at determining that and then sending you along to the right treatment provider.”

Sleep psychologists are a great resource if you want to try other treatment options before turning to medication. The American Psychological Association has a psychologist finder where you can enter your zip code and search specifically for sleep psychologists in your area. You could also check with your insurance provider or ask your PCP if they know of any sleep psychologists near you.

Many people start trying to fix their sleep with supplements like melatonin or magnesium. They might turn to their primary care doctor next and either try a medication and love the results, or feel a little stuck because they don’t want meds, but there’s not much else being offered.

If there is an underlying medical cause for your sleeplessness, like restless legs syndrome or sleep apnea, treating that condition should alleviate the insomnia. For everyone else, Meers says medication can be a wonderful tool, but treatment should start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I.

“That’s what the research shows is most effective. So when somebody comes to me, I’m like, ‘I want you to do what’s going to be most effective for you.’ And so my goal is to start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia.”

CBT-I is very different from cognitive behavioral therapy to treat something like anxiety or depression. It helps bridge the connection between your biology and your psychology, Meers says.

“The way that cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia works is that we are using our understanding of the biology of sleep to get your behaviors in line with your biology. We are not just focusing on sleep timing, but also how your body has learned to sleep poorly and how do we unlearn that.”

CBT-I is actually a pretty short treatment, compared to most plans in the field of psychology — an average of just four to eight sessions, says Meers.

“It’s very skills-based, meaning I’m teaching a lot of skills in the first four sessions, and then for the next few sessions, we’re just tracking our progress and seeing how things are working. You are changing a lot of your habits, and you’re changing those habits in the service of retraining your body and your mind to associate the bed with sleep. I’m literally telling people to get out of bed, here’s what you do when you get out of bed, here’s what to think about, and then here’s when you get into bed, here’s your sleep schedule for the next week.”

The moral of the story is that you shouldn’t wait to tell someone — your PCP, a sleep psychologist, your usual therapist — about your sleep struggles. Whether you want to try CBT-I, find a medication that works for you, or investigate a possible issue like sleep apnea, there is help out there for sleeplessness.

#7898. What’s up, Butt? What a Cat’s Trying to Say With Their Derrière in the Air

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange new behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

As âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

The insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

The most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

However, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

On its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

Some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

There are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

Urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

At the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral issues, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

Keeping her indoors is especially important during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

Responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

Until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

Why wait until spring? Planting fruit trees before winter gives the a chance to establish their roots before the growing season gets underway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree. ("À la Sainte-Catherine, tout bois prend racine.”) That may not apply literally to every tree species, but I can tell you this much: November is an excellent time to plant many kinds of fruit trees as long as the ground is not frozen.

Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving. Each tree in your home orchard can provide delicious homegrown harvests for years to come. Planting fruit trees in November offers many benefits. The cooler late-fall weather reduces transplanting stress, and seasonal rains keep the soil moist. That helps the trees establish roots before spring growth begins.

Which fruit trees should top your list? Many wonderful fruit trees are great to plant in November, so choose the one that grows your favorite fruit. But be sure to consider your local climate. Each fruit tree species has its own hardiness zone that indicates its cold tolerance. Some – like apples and pears – also have winter chilling requirements. You’ll also want to consider the mature size of the tree and be certain it will fit into your landscape.

Does life get any better than wandering out to the backyard and pulling a crisp apple right off your own tree and taking a bite? So when you consider planting a tree in November, don’t overlook apples. Apple trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–8, depending on the variety. You can plant either a bare-root apple tree or a container-grown tree in November, as long as the soil is not frozen, although spring planting is often safer in colder zones 3–4.

There are many apple varieties to choose from. Most won’t fruit reliably on their own, so check their pollination requirements when you purchase your tree. Your tree may require a compatible cross-pollinator that flowers at the same time. For a great pairing, try a ‘Honeycrisp’ apple tree alongside a ‘Gala’ apple tree – both available from Trees.com – which can cross-pollinate and give you two delicious varieties to harvest. If you only have room for one tree, ‘Golden Delicious’ is partially self-fertile and can produce fruit without a partner, although you'll generally get a better crop with cross-pollination.

Plant your apple tree in a full sun location in well-draining soil. You may want to stake the tree to prevent any windrock until its roots anchor it well. You can buy a tree-staking kit from Amazon, but if your area is very windy, a crossbar attached to two posts will provide more support.

Pears feel like a fancier fruit than apples, but the trees are just as easy to grow and maintain. Like pear slices in your salad? With your own pear tree, you can pick sweet fruit anytime during the harvest season. Pear trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–10, depending on the variety.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Like apple trees, pear trees grow best in a full sun location in well-draining soil. As with most apple trees, pear trees are not usually self-pollinating. That means that you will need two compatible cultivars for reliable pollination and fruit set. However, there are exceptions. Both the ‘Bartlett’ pear tree and ‘Kieffer’ pear tree, available from Garden Goods Direct, are partially self-fertile, although they generally produce better crops with a suitable pollination partner. Kieffer also offers good resistance to fire blight, making it worth considering in areas where this disease is a concern.

November can be a good time to plant a bare-root pear tree in milder regions. The plant is dormant, but its root system can continue to grow during the winter as long as the soil remains sufficiently warm and unfrozen. It is also possible to plant container trees in November. Be sure the planting hole is several times as wide as the root system, but no deeper than the root ball.

If you want a tree with sweet, juicy fruit, consider planting a plum tree. The fruit is delicious when eaten fresh, but also makes great compotes or jams. Plum trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 4–9, depending on the variety. November is a good month to plant bare-root plum trees in milder regions, and it’s suitable for container-grown plum trees as well. Just don’t wait too long since you can't plant after the ground is frozen. In colder zones, spring planting is often safer.

Most fruit trees need sunny locations, and plum trees are not an exception. In fact, it’s particularly important to select a good site since plums flower very early in spring. If your tree is in a low-lying frost pocket, the blossoms will be vulnerable to late frosts. You should also pick a site that offers protection from harsh winds. Plant your plum in cool, well-draining soil. Wet, heavy soil can lead to root disease.

Most plum trees require a pollinator, so you’ll need to plant two compatible trees. However, several varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree is enough to produce a harvest. One great option is the ‘Methley’ plum tree, available from Trees.com, which produces sweet, juicy fruit without needing a pollination partner.

Most of us know that a peach tree is a deciduous tree with juicy round fruits. Here’s a lesser-known fact: the same botanical species can grow fuzzy fruits, called peaches, or glossy-skinned fruits, called nectarines. Peach trees generally thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5–8, although this varies by variety. Peach trees, especially bare-root peach trees, can be successfully planted in November, as long as the ground is not frozen. In colder regions, however, spring planting is often safer.

Peach trees need sunny sites. Plant yours where it will get at least 6–8 hours a day of direct sun. This is essential to trigger flower buds and sweeten the fruit. The soil should be well-draining since standing water will rot the tree’s roots. If the tree is grafted, be sure to set the tree in the planting hole so that the graft union sits above the soil line.

Peach trees also need a specific amount of winter cold, chill hours, when temperatures fall within the range of approximately 32°F to 45°F (0°C to 7°C). Standard peach varieties need from 650 to 1,050 chill hours, although you can find low-chill types that need as few as 100 hours.

One great option for colder regions is the ‘Red Haven’ peach tree from Trees.com, a self-fertile variety that produces sweet, juicy peaches and needs around 800–900 chill hours. For warmer regions with mild winters, try ‘Tropic Snow,’ a low-chill variety that needs just 225 chill hours and produces deliciously sweet, white-fleshed peaches.

The American persimmon is among our most overlooked native fruit trees. This species does not get the spotlight given to apple, peach, or pear trees, yet it offers so much: edible fruit, wildlife habitat, and attractive fall foliage. The fruit is an important food source for wild birds and mammals, including raccoons, opossums, and foxes, and it remains available into early winter, when many other food sources have diminished.

Native to the eastern and southeastern United States, these trees are very cold-hardy, thriving in USDA hardiness zones 4–9. You can buy a common American persimmon tree from Plant Addicts to enjoy its fruit and seasonal interest in your own backyard. American persimmons typically have separate male and female trees, but some varieties are self-fertile and can produce fruit without a pollination partner. If you're growing a tree for its fruit, check its pollination requirements before buying.

The trees can grow to between 35 and 60 feet (10–18 m) tall, although they can be kept smaller by pruning. The fruit they produce is orange and initially astringent, but it becomes sweet and delicious when it fully ripens, often around the time of the first frost.

November is a good time to plant an American persimmon tree in milder regions. You cannot plant at this time, however, if the ground is frozen. Find a well-drained area with loamy, organically rich soil in a full sun location. Avoid frost pockets since these trees may be damaged by unseasonable frosts.

Fig trees have a long and somewhat exotic history. They have been cultivated for 12,000 years and are among the earliest domesticated plants. They have deep symbolic meaning as symbols of peace and prosperity, but, perhaps more important to modern gardeners, the trees are tough, drought-tolerant, and resistant to pests and diseases.

Fig trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 6–11, depending on the variety, although those in colder zones may need winter protection. For a reliable, sweet-fruited variety, try the ‘Brown Turkey’ fig from Nature Hills, which is well suited to milder regions. Gardeners in colder zones might prefer the ‘Chicago Hardy’ fig, also available from Nature Hills, which can withstand much lower winter temperatures with suitable protection. Both varieties are self-fruitful, so you only need one tree to enjoy a harvest.

If you live in USDA zone 8 or above, it is generally appropriate to plant your tree in November, provided the ground isn't frozen. In cooler zones, you should wait until spring. For November planting, select a full-sun location, ideally against a south- or southwest-facing wall. This helps the tree capture and retain warmth. The soil must be well-draining and slightly acidic. Water the tree deeply right after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

Once the tree is planted, apply a layer of organic mulch around the base, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the actual trunk to prevent rot.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7895. Nobody Warned Me About Bladder Leaks Before Becoming a Mom — Here's What I Wish I'd Known

For starters, they’re more common than you’d think.

After having my second baby, my body was a mess: hair falling out, boobs engorged — the works. So when I peed a little when I sneezed, it didn’t seem like a big deal. Until it happened again. And again. Eventually, I managed to sneeze, cough, and laugh without feeling some bladder leakage, but it took a few months for my body to get the memo.

These days, everyone talks about their pelvic floor: what it is, how to strengthen it, how having a baby can wreck it. But bladder leakage — which can be related to that all-important pelvic floor and the stress it undergoes during pregnancy and labor — tends to fly under the radar. No one wants to talk about it, maybe because there’s still a stigma attached to bathroom issues. Even though I’ve discussed every other postpartum thing under the sun (padsicles! Peri bottles! Nipple shields!) with my friends, urinary incontinence has never entered the chat.

But fortunately, Poise is ready to. The brand’s variety of bladder-leakage pads makes it easy to find exactly what you want, be it feels-like-you’re-wearing-nothing protection or a pad that keeps you dry all day. With that, here’s everything I wish someone had warned me about ahead of time.

Bladder leakage might not come up a lot (or at all) in the group chat, but a lot of women experience it. In fact, a large scientific review found that one in three women experiences bladder leakage between six weeks and a year after giving birth — whether it’s their first child or their third. So you’re probably not the only mom at the baby music class who’s dealing with the occasional accident. It only seems like a rarity because no one talks about it, when really it’s a legitimate and very normal part of recovering from birth. And that’s a disservice, because when people aren’t comfortable talking about issues like this, then the solutions don’t receive attention, either.

So you have some accidental leakage and want to give your old period pads a shot. While your average maxi-pad might do the trick if your leak is small, do you really want to risk an impromptu pants change while you’re out and about with your baby? If not, then you might need to consider more protection with a pad that’s actually designed for bladder leaks, like Poise's Pads for Bladder Leaks.

Poise’s pads quickly absorb wetness and trap odor so that no one but you knows what you're dealing with, and they come with layers that wick moisture and keep you feeling dry. On top of up to 12 hours of protection, they stay 25 times drier than the leading period pad. Plus, Poise Bladder Leak Pads have a thoughtful, contoured design that prevents bunching — so you can wear them under leggings and no one will know the difference.

A pad that can handle bladder leakage might sound huge, bulky, and like a wedgie waiting to happen. After all, super-thick pads can get tricky when you’re exercising, might need adjustment when you’re out and about, or can just be flat-out be annoying to wear.

But you don’t actually have to sacrifice comfort for protection. Poise Ultra Thin Pads for Bladder Leaks with Wings can handle moderate bladder leaks, absorbing wetness and neutralizing odors so you feel (and smell) fresh all day. They have layers that have been specifically designed to handle more wetness and help you stay dry, so you can focus on more important things, like enjoying postpartum life!

Bladder leaks after baby make a lot of sense, considering the many ways in which pushing a kid out can affect with your body. But (sorry in advance!) they can also occur at other times in your life, too — like during the menopause transition. It's not that perimenopause itself leads to bladder leakage, but natural changes in your body during this time, such as weight gain and anxiety, can contribute to it, according to one study.

And, as you can imagine when you have a baby bouncing around on top of your bladder (and frequently kicking it), leakage can also happen during pregnancy itself — not just after delivery. It’s actually more common than it is postpartum: Roughly four in 10 women experience bladder leakage during pregnancy, according to one analysis.

This is all to say: Bladder leaks are a normal part of life, whether you’re having a baby, recently gave birth, or are just getting older. And when that happens, it’s a relief to have protection that you can count on — and actually feel confident and comfortable wearing. After all, there are a lot of things to worry about when you become a mom; having to swap out your underwear shouldn’t be one of them.

#7894. Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

By Cassie Shortsleeve Updated Nov. 24, 2026

Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

She never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

The two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

“Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood says.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

While a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

For Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”

Today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

“People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”

When she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an issue she’d work on.

In 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an issue that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she says. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”

Rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”

Rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this issue.’”

She also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and says, ‘This is important to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

“Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood says. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”

What that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.)

Rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.)

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood says. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”

#7893. Let’s Be SMART – Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

This easy DIY combines rose hips, seed heads, and garden foliage to create a beautiful natural decoration that's a treat for winter birds, too.

Seasonal wreaths are popular décor for the front door, porches, patios, and decks. Stores offer a lot of options, from plastic wreaths to pricier products made from natural materials. But why spend money on these? Your backyard likely contains almost everything you need to make your own holiday wreath.

And while you’re crafting a gorgeous natural wreath, why not help birds in winter? Backyard birds have far fewer natural resources to exploit in the cold, so any support you can provide benefits these garden friends. By being thoughtful about what you put in your natural wreath, you can enjoy seasonal décor and support birds.

Making a winter wreath for birds that is also beautiful isn’t difficult. Here's what you’ll need and how to put it all together to make a bird feeder wreath you can display all year. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then don't miss our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

The first step in making a wreath is to gather materials. You’ll want evergreen cuttings for the wreath's foundation, plus attractive decorative items that also feed birds. Avoid any plants that have been treated with pesticides. You can make an exclusively rose hip wreath or seed head wreath, or mix and match elements within one wreath. Here’s what to look for in the garden:

The foundation of your wreath will be a base made from the flexible stems and sticks you gathered. You’ll also need twine or florist wire, like this Pauleen wire, and pruning shears or sharp, sturdy scissors. If you are short on time or materials, you can also buy a willow or grapevine base at a craft or garden store – this 14-Inch Grapevine Wreath from Amazon is ideal. Making your own isn’t difficult, though:

Don’t worry about making your wreath perfectly symmetrical. You can hide some flaws with the added elements.

This is the creative part of the project. Exactly where and how you add the decorative elements is up to you, but start with evergreens:

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

How you arrange the elements is totally up to your taste and creative mood. You can do a wreath loaded with rose hips or with a little bit of everything arranged so that you can still see a lot of the evergreens. As you design your wreaths, consider both aesthetics and how birds will use it. Avoid synthetic décor, like glitter or plastic berries, which could also harm birds.

Your wreath is holiday décor, but it’s also for the birds, so find somewhere to hang it where they can find it and feed safely on it. A sheltered position is best to protect birds from strong winds and predators. It should also be visible, so birds can find it, not too tucked away. If it is more out in the open, place the wreath near a sheltered area, so birds can quickly dart between the wreath and shelter.

It’s also important to consider window safety. You might want the wreath in a spot you can see from inside, but don’t place it so close to windows that birds risk a deadly collision.

A bird feeder wreath might start out as Christmas décor, but it can offer visual interest and feed all winter if you take good care of it:

A holiday wreath can be so much more than a temporary piece of Christmas decoration. Decorate for the entire winter with a natural wreath that also supports your local wildlife. Gather from your own garden and talk to neighbors if you need more materials. Experiment with any natural food source in your area, from various berries and rose hips to all kinds of seedheads and pinecones. And then, enjoy the show.

#7891. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! My Elderly Dog is Drinking and Urinating A Lot! (October 19, 2026)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

Dr. Paola Cuevas is our Senior In-House Veterinarian at Dogster and Pangolia. She has over 19 years of experience working with an array of species and loves sharing her knowledge and experience with our readers and aims to provide assistance with any issue presented by your non-human family members. She received her degree from the University of Guadalajara, Mexico.

Her passions are animal welfare and preventive medicine, and has skills in the fields of nutrition, microscopy, clinical pathology, diagnostic imaging, and endoscopy. Paola frequently contributes pet care insight to various media outlets like PetMD, The Daily Record, Parents.com, etc.

Paola is also an animal behaviorist with extensive experience in positive reinforcement animal training.

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

To start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. While modern cat food isnât likely to be venomous, your cat's instincts still tell them to beware anything they havenât eaten before.

Itâs the combination of a desire for the familiar and a tendency to get bored of the too familiar that makes picky cats so hard to feed. They want enough options that fall within a very specific range of flavors, textures, and aromas to keep them both interested and comfortable.

This can make adding moisture to their diets challenging, too, especially for cats who prefer dry food over wet. Luckily, simple additions like savory bone broth can help cat parents incorporate more moisture without introducing an entirely unfamiliar meal.

Cats may not be the ones cooking dinner, but they certainly have opinions about what's in their bowls. Inspired by his own discerning feline companion, a Maine Coon named Nacho, lifelong cat dad and celebrity chef Bobby Flay created Made by Nacho to give cats a menu of their own.

With multiple tasty dry and wet food recipes, plus numerous additions to keep mealtime poppinâ, Made by Nacho makes it easy to add just the right amount of variety to keep your kitty interested and comfortable.
